mainTopic: Parting words to the dead and the living, and going 'from strength to strength' to close the מסכת
overview: This last amud of מסכת מועד קטן opens with the end of a statement from the previous page. That statement compares something very hard to a rope being forced through a narrow ring, and it comes in two versions. Then רבי לוי בר חייתא teaches how to say goodbye. To a dead person you say 'לֵךְ בְּשָׁלוֹם' (go IN peace), and to a living person you say 'לֵךְ לְשָׁלוֹם' (go TO peace). The גמרא proves the first half from a פסוק about אברהם. It proves the second half from two stories: דוד told אבשלום 'go in peace' and it ended badly, while יתרו told משה 'go to peace' and משה succeeded. Next, רבי לוי teaches that whoever goes between the בית הכנסת and the בית המדרש merits to greet the שכינה, based on 'They go from strength to strength.' רב reads the same פסוק to mean that תלמידי חכמים never stop rising, even in עולם הבא. The amud closes with the הדרן, finishing the perek and the whole מסכת.

steps.title: Two versions of a comparison: like a rope pulled through a narrow ring
steps.stepSummary: The end of a statement from the previous page. Something extremely hard is compared to a knotted rope passing through a narrow ring. רבי יוחנן gives a slightly different image: a thick rope through that ring.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is as hard as a knotted rope passing through a narrow ring. רבי יוחנן said: as hard as a thick ship's rope passing through a narrow ring.
steps.whatsHappening: We are joining in the middle. These are the closing words of a statement from the previous page that describes how hard and painful something is, and two versions of the picture are given.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both versions use the same idea: something bulky being forced through a tight opening. The first version says a knotted rope. רבי יוחנן says a thick rope, like the ones used on a ship. The point of both is the same, extreme difficulty; only the image changes slightly.

keyTerms.meaning: A knotted or tangled rope (here; not 'birds')
Here: a narrow ring or eyelet that a rope runs through

steps.confusionAlert: In most places וֶושֶׁט means the food pipe, and צִיפּוֹר means a bird. Here both words are part of a picture of a rope being pulled through a tight ring.

phrases.english: Like a knotted rope through the opening of a narrow ring.
phrases.notes: These words finish a sentence that began on the previous page.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said:
Like a thick ship's rope through the opening of a narrow ring.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues a statement from the previous page, offering two versions of the same comparison.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The difficulty is like forcing a rope (knotted, or thick per רבי יוחנן) through a narrow ring.

steps.title: How to say goodbye to the dead and to the living
steps.stepSummary: רבי לוי בר חייתא rules that when you part from the dead you say 'לֵךְ בְּשָׁלוֹם', and when you part from the living you say 'לֵךְ לְשָׁלוֹם'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי לוי בר חייתא said: someone leaving a dead person should not say 'go to peace' but 'go in peace.' Someone leaving a living person should not say 'go in peace' but 'go to peace.'
steps.whatsHappening: A new teaching begins. רבי לוי בר חייתא gives a rule about the exact words to use when saying goodbye.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The difference is one small letter: ב (in) versus ל (to). For the dead, the right wording is 'in peace.' For the living, it is the opposite: 'to peace.' The reasons come in the next two steps.

keyTerms.meaning: One who takes leave of someone, saying goodbye
'Go to peace,' the proper goodbye to a living person
'Go in peace,' the proper goodbye to a dead person

steps.whyThisMatters: This became a well-known practical custom: be careful to say 'לֵךְ לְשָׁלוֹם' when parting from a living person.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Levi bar Chayta said:
One who takes leave of a dead person,
should not say to him, 'Go to peace,'
but rather, 'Go in peace.'
One who takes leave of a living person,
should not say to him, 'Go in peace,'
but rather, 'Go to peace.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new teaching, not connected to the rope comparison.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: To the dead say 'לֵךְ בְּשָׁלוֹם'; to the living say 'לֵךְ לְשָׁלוֹם'.

steps.title: Source for 'in peace' for the dead: what ה׳ told אברהם
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא repeats the first half of the rule and supports it with the פסוק where ה׳ tells אברהם, 'You shall come to your fathers in peace.'
steps.simpleTranslation: For the dead you say 'go in peace,' because the פסוק says: 'And you shall come to your fathers in peace.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא repeats the rule about the dead so it can give the source for it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this פסוק ה׳ tells אברהם about his death, and the word used is 'בְּשָׁלוֹם' (in peace). Since the Torah uses 'in peace' when speaking about death, that is the right wording for someone who has died.

keyTerms.meaning: Your fathers, meaning your ancestors who have passed away

phrases.aramaic: הַנִּפְטָר מִן הַמֵּת, לֹא יֹאמַר לוֹ ״לֵךְ לְשָׁלוֹם״,
phrases.english: One who takes leave of a dead person should not say to him, 'Go to peace,'
but rather, 'Go in peace,'
as it is said:
'And you shall come to your fathers in peace.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source for the first half of the rule in step 2.
steps.raayaObject: The rule that the dead are told 'לֵךְ בְּשָׁלוֹם'.
steps.raayaSupportSource: בראשית 15:15, where אברהם is told he will come to his fathers 'בְּשָׁלוֹם'.

steps.title: Source for 'to peace' for the living: דוד and אבשלום versus יתרו and משה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא repeats the second half of the rule. It supports it with two stories: דוד told אבשלום 'go in peace' and אבשלום ended up hanged, while יתרו told משה 'go to peace' and משה succeeded.
steps.simpleTranslation: For the living you say 'go to peace.' דוד said to אבשלום 'go in peace,' and he went and was hanged. יתרו said to משה 'go to peace,' and he went and succeeded.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא repeats the rule about the living and backs it up by comparing two goodbyes in תנ״ך and how each one turned out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof works by contrast. 'In peace' was said to a living person (אבשלום) and he came to a bad end. 'To peace' was said to a living person (משה) and he succeeded. So the living should be told 'לְשָׁלוֹם', and 'בְּשָׁלוֹם' is the wording that fits the dead.
steps.whatToRemember: Dead: 'לֵךְ בְּשָׁלוֹם' (from the פסוק about אברהם). Living: 'לֵךְ לְשָׁלוֹם' (משה succeeded after hearing it, while אבשלום, who heard 'בְּשָׁלוֹם', was hanged).

phrases.aramaic: הַנִּפְטָר מִן הַחַי, לֹא יֹאמַר לוֹ ״לֵךְ בְּשָׁלוֹם״,
phrases.english: One who takes leave of a living person should not say to him, 'Go in peace,'
but rather, 'Go to peace,'
for behold, David, who said to Avshalom
'Go in peace,'
he went and was hanged;
Yisro, who said to Moshe, 'Go to peace,'
he went and succeeded.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source for the second half of the rule in step 2, matching the proof for the first half in step 3.
steps.raayaObject: The rule that the living are told 'לֵךְ לְשָׁלוֹם'.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The contrast between דוד's 'לֵךְ בְּשָׁלוֹם' to אבשלום (who was hanged) and יתרו's 'לֵךְ לְשָׁלוֹם' to משה (who succeeded).

steps.title: Going from the בית הכנסת to the בית המדרש brings a person close to the שכינה
steps.stepSummary: רבי לוי teaches that whoever goes from the בית הכנסת to the בית המדרש, or the other way around, merits to greet the שכינה, based on the פסוק 'They go from strength to strength.'
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי לוי said: Anyone who goes from the בית הכנסת to the בית המדרש, or from the בית המדרש to the בית הכנסת, merits to greet the שכינה. As it says: 'They go from strength to strength, he appears before God in Zion.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another teaching from רבי לוי. It praises a person who goes straight from davening to learning, or from learning to davening.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק describes people going 'from strength to strength' and then 'appearing before God.' רבי לוי reads the two 'strengths' as the two holy places, the בית הכנסת and the בית המדרש. A person who keeps moving from one to the other gets to 'appear before God,' which means greeting the שכינה.

keyTerms.meaning: The synagogue, the place of תפילה
The study hall, the place of learning תורה
The 'face' of the Divine Presence; being close to ה׳

phrases.english: And רבי לוי said:

phrases.aramaic: כׇּל הַיּוֹצֵא מִבֵּית הַכְּנֶסֶת לְבֵית הַמִּדְרָשׁ,
phrases.english: Anyone who goes out from the synagogue to the study hall,
or from the study hall to the synagogue,
merits to greet the Divine Presence,
as it says:
"They go from strength to strength,"
phrases.notes: תהלים 84:8. The two 'strengths' are the shul and the study hall.

phrases.english: "he appears before God in Zion."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another teaching from the same רבי לוי, moving from the topic of parting words to praise for going between תפילה and learning.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Moving from the בית הכנסת to the בית המדרש, or back, earns a person closeness to the שכינה.

steps.title: תלמידי חכמים never stop going higher, even in עולם הבא
steps.stepSummary: רב חייא בר אשי quotes רב: תלמידי חכמים have no rest even in עולם הבא, using the same פסוק, 'They go from strength to strength.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חייא בר אשי said in the name of רב: תלמידי חכמים have no rest, even in עולם הבא. As it says: 'They go from strength to strength, he appears before God in Zion.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second teaching on the very same פסוק. Here it describes תלמידי חכמים in עולם הבא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי לוי used the פסוק for movement in this world. רב applies it to תלמידי חכמים forever: they keep going 'from strength to strength' and never stop growing, even in עולם הבא. Here 'no rest' is praise, because they always keep climbing higher.
steps.confusionAlert: 'No rest' does not mean they suffer. It means they never stop rising in learning and closeness to ה׳.
steps.whatToRemember: The מסכת ends on a hopeful note: a person who serves ה׳ keeps going 'from strength to strength,' in this world and in the next.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב חִיָּיא בַּר אָשֵׁי אָמַר רַב:
phrases.english: רב חייא בר אשי said in the name of רב:
Torah scholars have no rest
even in the World to Come,
as it says:
"They go from strength to strength,"
phrases.notes: This is the same פסוק רבי לוי just used. Here it means they keep climbing forever.

phrases.english: "he appears before God in Zion."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חִיָּיא בַּר אָשֵׁי אָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the same פסוק as step 5 for a new teaching: endless spiritual growth for תלמידי חכמים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: תלמידי חכמים never stop growing, even in עולם הבא.
steps.whyThisMatters: Ending the מסכת this way teaches that finishing a מסכת is not a stopping point. A learner keeps going to the next level.

steps.title: Hadran — Closing the perek ואלו מגלחין and מסכת מועד קטן
steps.stepSummary: The closing formula for the third perek, ואלו מגלחין, and for the entire מסכת מועד קטן.
steps.simpleTranslation: We will return to you, ואלו מגלחין, and מסכת מועד קטן is complete.
steps.whatsHappening: This is not part of the discussion. It is the traditional line said when finishing a perek, and here it also marks the end of the whole מסכת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'הדרן עלך' means 'we will return to you.' It promises that we will come back and learn this perek again. The second half announces that the whole מסכת מועד קטן is finished.

keyTerms.meaning: We will return to you; said when finishing a perek

steps.whatToRemember: With this line we have finished מסכת מועד קטן, and we promise to come back and learn it again.

phrases.english: We will return to you, ואלו מגלחין,
phrases.notes: ואלו מגלחין is the name of this perek, taken from its opening words.

phrases.english: and מסכת מועד קטן is complete.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Formally closes the perek and the מסכת after the final teachings.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The perek ואלו מגלחין and the whole מסכת מועד קטן are complete, with a promise to return to them.
